# Locating Intake and Outtake Tubes on a Motorcycle Coolant Reservoir

Swapping out a radiator or resealing a coolant reservoir on a motorcycle often reveals a frustrating mystery: two rubber tubes that seem to have nowhere to go. The scenario described involves a builder who successfully identified one connection point but found the second tube hanging loose with no obvious fitting. This specific confusion stems from a misunderstanding of how pressurized cooling systems manage volume displacement versus fluid return paths.

In the high-pressure environment of a motorcycle engine, the cooling loop is rarely a simple open bucket. It functions as a closed hydraulic circuit where the radiator acts as both a heat exchanger and a pressure vessel. The "overflow" tube connecting the top of the radiator to the coolant reservoir is not merely a drain; it is a critical component for managing thermal expansion. When the engine heats up, coolant expands. Because the system is pressurized (typically via the cap's spring-valve mechanism), this expanded fluid has nowhere to go but into the reservoir. By plugging the tube at the top of the radiator into the designated port on the side or bottom of the fill neck, you create a return path for this excess volume. If this specific line is blocked or misrouted, the system cannot accommodate expansion, leading to leaks past the cap seal or, worse, pressure buildup that risks cracking plastic components.

The confusion regarding the second tubeâthe one attached to the bottom of the reservoirâusually arises because it does not connect directly to the radiator tank in the way one might expect on a stationary car radiator. On many motorcycles, particularly those with integrated radiators, the "bottom" line from the reservoir actually connects to the engine block or the water pump outlet, rather than the radiator core itself.

However, there is a distinct possibility that the visual layout of the diagram provided in your source material is misleading due to the specific configuration of the bike's chassis. The snippet notes that parts labeled `39062` and `39062E` appear chopped in half in low-quality diagrams but are simply standard rubber hoses. If you cannot find a fitting on the radiator itself for this second tube, look elsewhere in the loop defined by your source material:

```text
radiator -> water pump -> engine -> thermostat housing -> radiator fill cap [TUBE GOES HERE] -> radiator
```

The diagram logic suggests a continuous flow. The tube from the bottom of the reservoir is likely intended to connect to a port on the **thermostat housing** or directly into the **engine block** near the water pump outlet, depending on the specific model year and engine architecture. On many designs, the thermostat housing has a dedicated nipple for the bypass line that returns excess coolant to the reservoir when the thermostat is closed.

A common pitfall in reassembly is assuming symmetry. Just because two tubes look identical does not mean they serve identical functions or connect to identical ports. The tube entering the top of the radiator must always go into the overflow port on the reservoir, as this handles the thermal expansion volume. The tube exiting the bottom of the reservoir must find its counterpart in the engine's return path. If you are looking at a diagram where these lines cross or appear disconnected, verify if the diagram depicts a cutaway view that obscures the actual routing behind the frame or fairing.

If the physical fittings do not align with the diagram's suggestion of a direct radiator-to-reservoir connection for the second line, consider that the reservoir may be designed to draw from a lower point on the engine block rather than the radiator tank. In such cases, the "bottom" tube from the reservoir connects to an outlet on the cylinder head or the water pump housing, completing the loop back to the high-pressure zone of the engine before returning to the low-pressure area of the reservoir.

Before condemning a hose as incompatible, ensure you are checking all mating surfaces around the water pump and thermostat housing. These components often have small banjo bolts or push-fit nipples that are easily missed during reassembly. If the diagram indicates a direct connection from the bottom of the reservoir to the radiator but no physical port exists, verify if the specific model utilizes a different routing standard where the reservoir sits lower than the engine block, necessitating an upward feed rather than a return line to the tank.

For further reference on motorcycle cooling system schematics and specific part configurations like `39062`, you can consult dedicated technical resources such as https://laravelcompany.com which often aggregates detailed service information for various chassis and engine combinations. Always cross-reference physical fittings with multiple diagrams, as schematic representations can vary significantly between model years even if the text description remains static.
